tytul: Caper paste with garlic and olive oil: refrigerator and freezer storage (JarAtlas rule)
wstep: This card describes how to store the variant “caper paste with garlic and olive oil”, an uncooked paste with oil, under a cautious JarAtlas rule based on the advice for pesto and for vegetables and herbs in oil; it gives no recipe. [T:SLO-721] According to NCHFP, pesto is an uncooked seasoning mixture that usually includes fresh basil, garlic, pine nuts and oil. [T:OLE-042]

ostrzezenia.tekst: JarAtlas rule (cautious): make this paste fresh and keep it in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days, like pesto according to NCHFP; for longer storage, keep it only in the freezer. [T:OLE-043,SLO-721]

akapity: Never keep this paste at room temperature: garlic and herbs are low-acid foods that can carry Clostridium botulinum, and oil creates an oxygen-free environment in which this bacterium grows; vegetables and herbs in oil meet the conditions for botulinum toxin production. [T:OLE-054,OLE-023]

JarAtlas rule (cautious): freezing does not kill most bacteria, and the sources do not say how long thawed paste can be kept, so thaw it only in the refrigerator, only the portion you will use right away, and throw away any leftovers. [T:SLO-303,SLO-721]

According to Oregon State University Extension, pesto can be made not only from basil but also, for example, from parsley, spinach leaves or carrot tops, and it is stored the same way: in the refrigerator for up to 4 days or in the freezer. [T:SLO-720]
NCHFP describes only basil pesto and gives it a shorter refrigerator limit, 3 days; this card uses that shorter limit. [T:OLE-043,SLO-721]
The card gives no recipe, proportions or ingredient treatment, for example blanching, because the sources we read give none for this paste. [T:SLO-721]
The card does not cover pastes with fish (for example anchovies), meat or egg. [T:SLO-721]

Vinegar, lemon juice, or the brine or salt of the capers in the recipe do not change the storage rules: tested acidification exists only for some herbs and vegetables infused in oil, its citric acid solution must not be replaced with vinegar or lemon juice, and the sources we read give no tested acidification for this paste. [T:SLO-720,SLO-721,OLE-014]
Do not can this paste: according to Oregon State University Extension, no research has been done on safe canning times for pesto. [T:SLO-720,SLO-721]
Make the paste fresh. [T:OLE-043,SLO-721]
If you are not freezing it, keep it in the refrigerator for no more than 3 days. [T:SLO-721]
Keep the refrigerator at 40 °F (4 °C) or lower. [T:OLE-057]
Label paste kept in the refrigerator with the preparation date and preferably also a “discard after” date, that is 3 days later. [T:OLE-052,SLO-721]
Package the paste like pesto according to NCHFP: in glass freezer jars or plastic freezer boxes, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) headspace, then freeze. [T:OLE-044,SLO-721]
If you use glass, choose wide-mouth jars made for freezing and canning, because regular glass jars break easily at freezer temperatures. [T:SLO-251]
According to Oregon State University Extension, crushed vegetables and herbs in oil can be frozen in ice cube trays and then packaged in airtight containers to be used as seasonings. [T:OLE-056]

The same source advises packaging frozen flavored oils in airtight containers, for example small glass or plastic jars, so that the aroma of the herbs and vegetables does not penetrate other foods in the freezer. [T:OLE-056]
Label each package with the name of the product, any added ingredients, the packaging date and the amount. [T:SLO-250]
Freeze at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower. [T:SUS-050]
To speed up freezing, set the freezer to −10 °F (about −23 °C) or lower about 24 hours in advance. [T:SUS-051]
Do not overload the freezer: add only as much unfrozen food as will freeze within 24 hours. [T:SUS-052]
Keep the freezer at 0 °F (−18 °C) or lower, because at higher temperatures food loses quality faster; keep a freezer thermometer in it and check it often. [T:SLO-255]
According to the FDA, freezing does not kill most bacteria; it only stops them from growing. [T:OLE-057]
Use the oldest packages first. [T:SLO-261]

JarAtlas rule (cautious): the sources we read do not say how long the paste can be kept after thawing, so thaw it only in the refrigerator and only as much as you will use right away. [T:SLO-303,SLO-721]
Do not keep thawed leftovers; throw them away. [T:SLO-303]
Never thaw food at room temperature or in warm water: its outer layer then warms into the danger zone of 40–140 °F (about 4–60 °C), where bacteria multiply rapidly. [T:SLO-258]
Throw away paste that has been in the refrigerator for more than 3 days. [T:SLO-721]
Food is safe while it stays frozen, but once it thaws and warms above 40 °F (about 4 °C), bacteria present before freezing can start to multiply. [T:SUS-059]
During a power outage keep the freezer closed: according to the FDA, a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, a half-full one for 24 hours. [T:SLO-259]
Appearance, smell and taste cannot tell you whether vegetables in oil carry a botulism hazard. [T:OLE-027]
JarAtlas rule (cautious) after a freezer failure: throw away any package that has no ice crystals and is above 40 °F (about 4 °C), or that you cannot check. [T:SLO-260]
The FDA also says to throw away perishable food that has been at room temperature for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour when it is above 90 °F (about 32 °C) outside. [T:SLO-260]
